newsitem.title: JAPAN: E.Asia buyers concerned over Canadian wheat delays.
newsitem.headline: E.Asia buyers concerned over Canadian wheat delays.

text.p: Major East Asian grain buyers said on Wednesday they are concerned about the current long delays in Canadian wheat shipments and are monitoring the situation, but generally have no immediate plans to switch to other sources.

Chicago wheat futures closed sharply up on Tuesday on talk U.S. suppliers might benefit by taking market share from Canada, where serious rail delays have kept more than 1.5 million tonnes of grain from reaching Pacific ports since January.

"We're closely monitoring shipments of Canadian wheat which have been delayed. But Japan currently has domestic wheat stocks equal to national consumption for 2.5 months," Japan's Food Agency trade division director Shinichi Yahagi said.
"We have no immediate plans to buy more U.S. wheat despite the shipment problems in Canada," Yahagi told Reuters.
Severe winter weather and legislated caps on rail rates for grain cargoes, which make it more profitable for Canadian rail companies to carry other commodities, lay behind the delays.

On Tuesday, 42 ocean vessels were waiting to load grain on Canada's Pacific coast, including 12 destined for Japan. Some had been waiting as long as 39 days. Another 13 ships were due to arrive later this week.
Yahagi earlier this month urged Tokyo representative of the Canadian Wheat Board to resolve the matter as soon as possible.
"We're ready to release some domestic stocks amid delays in the arrival of Canadian wheat," Yahagi said.
The Food Agency, the grain trading arm of the Agriculture Ministry, is Japan's sole importer of wheat, barley and rice.

The agency is a major buyer of Canadian wheat grade 1CW, which is mainly used for making bread, and has bought 107,000 tonnes of 1CW for February shipment and 87,000 tonnes for March shipment, another agency official said.
In South Korea, most grain buyers, who are not heavily dependent on Canadian grain, shrugged off news of the shipping problems.

Local flour mills carry wheat stocks for one-and-a-half months, an official with one of the major mills said, adding that, if necessary, South Korean firms could substitute Canadian western red spring with U.S. dark northern spring wheat.
South Korean mills have jointly bought 14,000 tonnes of Canadian wheat for shipment in February and another 20,000 tonnes for shipment in April, traders said.
"We expect the February shipment to be delayed about 10 days," the flour mill official said.
"We hope our cargo will not to be delayed further, but our purchases of Canadian wheat are steady and the quantities involved are smaller than those of other buyers," he said.
He added that his company had already conveyed its concerns over the shipping delays to its supplier.
According to Korea Flour Mills Industrial Association (KFMIA) data, total wheat imports by South Korean mills totalled 2,276,605 tonnes in 1996.
A KFMIA official said the U.S. supplied 1,553,010 tonnes, (68 percent), Australia 650,792 tonnes (29 percent), and Canada 72,803 tonnes (three percent).
Local feed millers said they were also not unduely copncerned by the Canadian delays as their purchases of feed grain from that origin were limited.
"At the moment we have no feed wheat imports from Canada," a trader with major buyer the National Livestock Cooperatives Federation (NLCF) said.
The NLCF imported 211,000 tonnes of feed wheat in 1996, from its total grain and oilseed imports of 3,768,654 tonnes.

A trader with a Seoul-based foreign firm said several South Korean feed mills had jointly bought two 50,000-tonne cargoes of Canadian feed wheat from Japanese trading house Mitsubishi Corp last December.

He said the companies had bought 50,000 tonnes of wheat at 86 cents per bushel C&F over the Chicago Board of Trade's March futures contract with shipment expected between February 9-28. Another 50,000 tonnes were purchased at 89 cents C&F over May futures with shipment set for March 12-31.

"Though we expect the first February shipment to be delayed about one week, we also expect the situation in Canada to return to normal when the second cargo is scheduled to be loaded," said an official representing the buyer companies.
In the Philippines, traders said they expected the Canadian situation to drive U.S. wheat prices even higher.

"(The delays) will affect delivery commitments of Canadian wheat. It will also affect the buying attitude of Asian buyers, including the Philippines," said Joanna Lim, a trader at Cargill Philippines Inc.
Manila traders said the Canadian problems could compel Asian buyers to look to alternative wheat suppliers such as Australia and the European Union.
They said they expected East Asian grains importers to particularly look to the European Union which is currently offering more competitive wheat prices than the U.S.
"But for Philippine buyers I still expect them to source the bulk of their orders from the United States because local bread makers prefer U.S. wheat," said one trader.
